trees.subject: Odd-only Eratosthenes sieve
trees.objective: Replace repeated per-number divisor scans with an odd-only Eratosthenes sieve sized from the runtime input. Mark composites from p*p with odd strides, sum exactly the primes through the inclusive limit, preserve argument validation and output, and measure the full implementation against the fixed benchmark while passing every supplied test.

nodes.hypothesis: Replacing repeated divisor scans with an odd-only sieve should reduce work substantially at the fixed benchmark, while runtime sizing and inclusive indexing preserve results for every valid limit. The baseline is correct but takes about 38.85 ms; the candidate's performance remains unmeasured.

retained: Replace per-number divisor scans with a runtime-sized odd-only Eratosthenes sieve.
Mark composites from p*p using odd-number index strides of p, then sum unmarked odd candidates and 2 when included.

nodes.hypothesis: The measured odd-only sieve was valid and averaged 0.00402 s versus the baseline's 0.03885 s. This candidate keeps that sieve mechanism but bounds its marking-prime loop with p <= limit/p, avoiding p*p overflow and stopping once further primes cannot mark a composite. Expect identical inclusive sums for every valid limit and, if the prior loop examined candidates beyond sqrt(limit), a small timing reduction; the performance effect is unmeasured. Stop if any supplied test fails or if confirmation measurements do not show a lower mean.

retained: Replace repeated per-number divisor scans with a runtime-sized array of odd-number composite flags; mark from p*p with odd-number index strides of p.
Bound the marking-prime loop with p <= limit/p so it stops after sqrt(limit) without multiplying for the condition; sum 2 separately and all unmarked odd candidates inclusively.

nodes.hypothesis: The two measured byte-flag sieve programs were correct at 0.0040196 s and 0.0039799 s; their roughly 1% gap in three samples does not establish a benefit from the loop-bound refinement. This contrasting experiment packs composite flags into 64-bit words while retaining odd-only indexing, marking from p*p by index strides of p, and inclusive summation. The smaller footprint could help cache behavior, but bit extraction and read-modify-write marking may instead cost time at the fixed 20,000 benchmark. Expect identical results for all valid inputs; stop if any supplied test fails or five-run confirmation does not beat the best measured byte-flag mean of 0.0039799 s. No speedup is assumed before measurement.

retained: Replace the byte-per-odd composite flags with a runtime-sized vector of packed 64-bit composite flags.
Retain overflow-safe marking-prime bound p <= limit/p, mark from p*p with odd-number index strides of p, and sum 2 plus every unmarked odd candidate through the inclusive limit.

nodes.hypothesis: The catalog contains three distinct valid programs: two byte-flag sieves averaging 0.0040196 s and 0.0039799 s, and a bit-packed sieve averaging 0.0040643 s. The bit-packed variant did not show a gain, and the small difference between byte variants is inconclusive. This contrasting experiment tests whether a runtime-sized mod-30 wheel, which stores only 8 candidates per 30 integers and marks p times wheel-gap quotients from p*p, reduces work enough to offset its indexing overhead at the fixed benchmark. No speedup is assumed; the performance result remains unmeasured.

retained: Replace the baseline divisor scans with a runtime-sized mod-30 wheel sieve using byte composite flags for the eight residues coprime to 30.

Mark composites beginning at p*p by iterating wheel-admissible quotients with the corresponding wheel gaps; sum 2, 3, and 5 separately and then all unmarked wheel candidates through the inclusive limit.

nodes.hypothesis: The catalog has four distinct valid programs; measured times are tightly grouped, with the best odd-only byte sieve at 0.0039799 s, the selected wheel parent at 0.0040110 s, and the bit-packed variant at 0.0040643 s. This contrasting experiment tests whether processing odd candidates in 4096-odd segments improves locality enough to offset base-prime setup and repeated per-segment marking at the fixed benchmark. No speedup is assumed; all valid limits remain runtime-sized and inclusive.

retained: Replace wheel indexing with an odd-only segmented sieve using runtime-derived base primes.
Sieve each segment from max(p*p, the first odd multiple of p in the segment), stepping by p in odd-index space, then sum unmarked values inclusively.
Preserve argument validation, accepted limit range, and output format.

nodes.hypothesis: The catalog reports five valid trials and five distinct programs with no repeats. The selected odd-only byte sieve is fastest at 0.0039799 s; the segmented, wheel, and bit-packed variants measured 0.0039908 s, 0.0040110 s, and 0.0040643 s respectively. Those close results do not establish that representation changes help. This contrasting experiment keeps the selected sieve but initializes the sum to the arithmetic total of odd candidates and subtracts each composite exactly once when first marked, testing whether eliminating the final candidate scan offsets the extra conditional work during marking. Correctness is intended to hold for every accepted limit; no speedup is assumed before measurement.

retained: Initialize the sum with 2 when included plus the arithmetic sum of all odd candidates through the inclusive limit.
During p-squared odd-stride marking, subtract a value only on its first composite mark, replacing the final full scan for unmarked candidates.

nodes.hypothesis: The catalog shows six distinct valid programs: the best byte odd-only sieve measured 0.0039799 s, the selected wheel parent 0.0040110 s, and the segmented variant 0.0039908 s. These close timings do not establish a gain. This experiment replaces the wheel mapping with direct odd-index byte slots, testing whether simpler indexing offsets any differences in marking and summation; no speedup is assumed.

retained: Replace the mod-30 wheel representation with a runtime-sized byte array for odd candidates starting at 3.
Mark odd composites from p*p using an index stride of p, stopping the marking-prime scan with the overflow-safe condition p > limit / p.
Sum unmarked odd values through the inclusive limit and add 2 when it is in range.

nodes.hypothesis: The catalog's best odd-only byte sieve measured 0.0039799 s; the segmented and bit-packed variants measured 0.0039908 s and 0.0040643 s. These close results and the earlier slower composite-subtraction experiment do not establish a gain. This contrasting candidate tests whether a branchless, four-accumulator sum over the byte sieve's odd candidates reduces scan cost enough to matter in the full benchmark. No speedup is assumed.

retained: Use a runtime-sized byte array for odd candidates and mark composites from p*p in odd-index strides of p.
Replace the conditional scalar summation pass with branchless candidate weighting and four independent partial sums, handling the remaining slots with a tail loop.

nodes.hypothesis: The catalog reports eight distinct valid programs and no repeats. The selected parent averages 0.0040196 s, the best byte-sieve variant 0.0039519 s, and the 4096-odd segmented variant 0.0039908 s; these close measurements do not establish that representation or segmentation caused the differences. This experiment tests whether using 16384-odd segments reduces repeated segment overhead enough to offset base-prime setup and per-segment work. It remains runtime-sized and inclusive; no speedup is assumed.

retained: Replace the single full-range odd composite array with a runtime-sized segmented odd-only sieve using 16384 odd candidates per segment.
Generate base primes through the integer square root of the validated limit; mark each segment from max(p*p, its first odd multiple), stepping by p in odd-index space.
Sum every unmarked odd candidate through the inclusive limit, add 2 when included, and preserve argument validation and output format.

nodes.hypothesis: The catalog contains nine distinct valid programs and no repeats. The best odd-byte sieve measured 0.0039519 s; the mod-30 wheel and bit-packed variants measured 0.0040110 s and 0.0040643 s, while segmented variants were near 0.00398–0.00399 s. These close measurements do not establish a representation advantage. This contrasting experiment tests whether a simpler runtime-sized mod-6 wheel, which stores two residues per six integers, reduces candidate marking and summation enough to offset residue-to-index mapping overhead. No speedup is assumed.

retained: Replace divisor scans with a runtime-sized byte sieve for candidates congruent to 1 or 5 modulo 6, marking 1 as composite and handling 2 and 3 separately.
For each unmarked candidate prime p, mark p times candidate quotients beginning at q=p (therefore p*p), advancing q through the 6k +/- 1 residues.
Sum every unmarked candidate through the inclusive runtime limit.

nodes.hypothesis: The catalog contains ten distinct valid programs. The best measured odd-byte sieve averages 0.0039519 s (cba6a7a3e818414a), while the 4096-odd segmented variant averages 0.0039908 s (5fe21186f8954287); these close measurements do not establish a causal advantage. This contrasting experiment tests whether a 16384-odd segment, effectively one segment at the fixed 20000 benchmark, reduces segmentation overhead enough to offset base-prime setup. No speedup is assumed.

retained: Replace per-number divisor scans with a runtime-sized odd-only Eratosthenes sieve.
Generate base primes through the integer square root of the runtime limit, then sieve 16384-odd chunks, starting each prime's marking at the greater of p*p and the first odd multiple in the chunk.
Sum every unmarked odd value through the inclusive limit, adding 2 when present; preserve the existing validation and output format.

nodes.hypothesis: The catalog has 11 distinct valid programs with no repeats; the best odd-byte sieve averaged 0.0039519 s (cba6a7a3e818414a), while the 16384-odd segmented variant averaged 0.0039753 s (1da5bb23da984306), with other structures also near 4 ms. These close measurements do not establish a causal advantage and suggest improvement has stalled. This experiment tests whether four-way unrolling of composite stores reduces loop-control overhead in the runtime-sized odd-only byte sieve enough to affect full-program timing. It preserves inclusive summation and validation; no speedup is assumed.

retained: Replace repeated divisor scans with a runtime-sized odd-only Eratosthenes sieve, marking from p*p at odd-number index strides of p.
Unroll composite marking four stores at a time, then handle remaining indices with a stride-p tail loop.
Sum unmarked odd candidates through the inclusive limit and add 2 when present, preserving argument validation and output.

nodes.hypothesis: The catalog reports 12 distinct valid programs and no repeats; the best odd-byte sieve averaged about 0.003951 s, while the 16384-odd segmented variant averaged about 0.003975 s. These close results do not establish a causal advantage, and the earlier four-way marking unroll did not clearly improve on the best. This experiment tests whether four-way unrolling of the final contiguous prime-sum scan reduces overhead while keeping the runtime-sized odd-only sieve, p*p marking, inclusive limit, validation, and output unchanged. No speedup is assumed.

retained: Replace repeated divisor scans with a runtime-sized odd-only byte sieve, marking composites from p*p at odd-index strides of p.
Unroll the final scan over unmarked odd candidates four ways, with a tail loop for all sizes.

trees.subject: Wheel-based incremental trial division
trees.objective: Develop and measure a distinct low-memory prime-generation alternative: enumerate candidates using a wheel that skips multiples of 2, 3, and 5, test each candidate only with previously found primes up to its square root, and accumulate the exact inclusive sum. Preserve the complete input/output contract and pass every supplied test; compare measured performance with the baseline without hard-coded answers or test-specific behavior.

nodes.hypothesis: The 30-wheel should avoid testing multiples of 2, 3, and 5, while restricting divisibility checks to discovered primes through the candidate's square root should sharply reduce work versus the baseline's full divisor scan. The baseline measured 0.03885 s; this program's relative performance remains unmeasured.

retained: Seed 2, 3, and 5, then enumerate only candidates in the 30-wheel sequence.
Test each candidate against previously found primes only through its square root, then add found primes to the exact inclusive sum.

nodes.hypothesis: The measured wheel/trial-division parent is correct at 0.0042003 s versus the correct baseline at 0.0388474 s; the catalog has only one distinct T2 program so far. Pre-reserving limit/8+3 prime slots should avoid vector growth at the benchmark size while retaining the same wheel, prior-prime square-root checks, and inclusive sum. Since divisibility checks likely dominate, expect a small or noisy timing change rather than assuming a gain. Stop this line if correctness fails or confirmation repeats do not show a consistent timing reduction.

retained: Reserve limit/8+3 entries in the prime vector before inserting seeds, reducing possible vector reallocations without changing the candidate wheel, divisor bound, or exact inclusive accumulation.

nodes.hypothesis: The correct wheel variants measured 0.00420 s and 0.00413 s versus the 0.03885 s baseline, but the reserve change alone does not establish a gain. This contrasting candidate stores only discovered primes up to floor(sqrt(limit)): every divisor needed for any candidate through limit remains available, while vector storage should shrink from O(pi(limit)) to O(pi(sqrt(limit))). Exact inclusive summation and the existing argument behavior remain unchanged. Expect correctness and lower prime-vector capacity; runtime effect is unknown and may be neutral or slower. Stop if any supplied test fails, or if confirmation shows a slowdown without a useful memory reduction.

retained: Enumerate candidates starting at 7 with the 30-wheel gap cycle, after summing the in-range seeds 2, 3, and 5.
Store discovered primes only through floor(sqrt(limit)); test each candidate using stored primes only through its square root and add every prime found to the inclusive uint64_t sum.
Preserve the existing argc, atoi, range-check, output, and exit behavior.

nodes.hypothesis: The three measured wheel variants are correct at about 4.13–4.21 ms versus the 38.85 ms baseline, while the prior square-root-limited-prime variant measured 4.208 ms and did not establish a speed gain. This contrasting version tests whether replacing the oversized dynamic prime vector with a fixed, bounded array (448 integers, under 1.8 KiB) reduces allocation/storage overhead while retaining the wheel, exact sum, and square-root-limited divisor set. Runtime impact remains unknown.

retained: Replace the dynamically allocated prime vector with a fixed 448-entry array sized safely for the 200000 input bound.
Keep the 30-wheel candidate enumeration and test candidates using previously discovered primes only through the candidate square root.
Retain discovered primes only when candidate <= limit / candidate, while adding every in-range prime to the exact inclusive sum.

nodes.hypothesis: The catalog reports four distinct, correct T2 programs, with wheel variants measuring about 4.13–4.20 ms versus the 38.85 ms baseline; the compact-storage variant measured 4.18 ms, so those storage changes have not shown a clear timing gain. This contrasting experiment keeps the 30-wheel and exact sum but starts trial division after the seeded 2, 3, and 5: the wheel already excludes their multiples, so their remainder checks are redundant. This may reduce work per candidate, but the timing effect is unmeasured and may be small or noisy.

retained: Retain the 30-wheel candidate sequence and inclusive uint64_t sum.
Begin each candidate's divisor scan at the first stored prime after 2, 3, and 5, which the wheel already excludes as factors.
Keep the square-root stopping condition and existing input, output, and exit behavior.

nodes.hypothesis: The five correct wheel variants measured about 4.13–4.20 ms versus the 38.85 ms baseline, with no clear timing gain from the tested storage and divisor-scan changes. This contrasting experiment replaces the 30-wheel gap cycle with a 210-wheel residue table: it excludes multiples of 7 as well as 2, 3, and 5, potentially reducing candidate and remainder work, while the larger table and nested iteration may offset that benefit. The performance effect is unknown pending controller measurement.

retained: Seed and sum in-range primes 2, 3, 5, and 7; enumerate further candidates from an ascending residue table for the 210-wheel, skipping multiples of 2, 3, 5, and 7.
Test each generated candidate against previously found primes after the wheel-excluded seeds, stopping when divisor > candidate / divisor; add every found prime to the inclusive uint64_t sum.
Preserve the existing argument count, atoi conversion, range check, output format, and exit behavior.

nodes.hypothesis: The selected parent stores discovered divisors as int even though the accepted limit caps every stored prime at floor(sqrt(200000)) = 447. Using uint16_t for this vector should halve its prime-data footprint without changing candidate enumeration, divisor checks, or the exact inclusive sum; any runtime effect is unknown. The catalog's correct wheel variants measured about 4.10–4.21 ms versus 38.85 ms for baseline, with no clear gain from prior storage or divisor-scan changes, so this experiment isolates representation width.

retained: Store only the discovered divisor primes in a vector of uint16_t; all stored primes are at most floor(sqrt(limit)), which is at most 447 under the accepted input bound.
Keep the 30-wheel candidate sequence, prior-prime trial division with the square-root stopping condition, exact uint64_t inclusive sum, and existing input/output behavior unchanged.

nodes.hypothesis: The catalog reports seven distinct, correct T2 programs; the 210-wheel candidate measured 0.004098 s versus the 0.038847 s baseline, while related storage and divisor-scan changes showed no clear gain. This experiment tests whether visiting the ordered residues of a 30-wheel block-by-block is preferable to a gap-cycle walk, while retaining only discovered primes that can divide values through the limit. The runtime effect is unknown until measured.

retained: Preserve the existing argc, atoi, range validation, uint64_t sum output, and exit behavior.
Enumerate candidates using ascending residues coprime to 30, grouped in blocks of 30; seed the sum with 2, 3, and 5 when in range.
Trial-divide each wheel candidate by previously discovered primes only, stopping beyond its square root; store a discovered prime only when it can be a divisor of a value through limit.

nodes.hypothesis: The catalog reports 8 distinct, correct T2 programs with no repeated programs; their measured means are about 4.10–4.21 ms versus the 38.85 ms baseline, so earlier wheel variants show little timing separation. This isolated experiment keeps the selected parent's 30-wheel enumeration and low-memory divisor storage, but replaces the per-divisor quotient bound with a square comparison. Because stored divisors are at most sqrt(limit) and limit is capped at 200000, the multiplication is safe; it may avoid runtime integer division, though its performance effect is unknown until measured.

retained: Preserve argument validation, inclusive uint64_t sum, output formatting, and exit behavior.
Retain the ascending 30-wheel residue enumeration and storage only of discovered primes that can divide values through the limit.
Replace the divisor > candidate / divisor stopping condition with divisor * divisor > candidate; the supported limit bounds the product safely.

nodes.hypothesis: The catalog reports nine distinct, correct T2 programs, with means clustered around 4.09–4.21 ms versus the 38.85 ms baseline. This experiment tests whether a single gap-cycle wheel walk paired with a bounded uint16_t stack buffer differs from the previously explored grouped-residue and dynamic-storage approaches. It preserves trial division by previously found primes through the square root and exact inclusive summation; any runtime or memory benefit remains unmeasured.

retained: Preserve the existing argument count, atoi parsing, accepted limit range, uint64_t sum, output format, and exit behavior.
Seed the inclusive sum with in-range primes 2, 3, and 5; enumerate subsequent candidates from 7 with the repeating 30-wheel gap cycle that skips multiples of 2, 3, and 5.

Use a bounded uint16_t array for previously discovered primes, trial-divide wheel candidates by stored primes after 2, 3, and 5 up to the square root, and store a discovered prime only when it can divide a candidate through the limit.

code_findings.mechanism: Faits du code : les arguments et la borne sont validés (lignes 7–10). Le vecteur ne représente que les impairs jusqu’à la limite; le crible part de p², marque par pas d’indice p et regroupe quatre écritures avant une boucle de fin (12–32). La somme ajoute 2 puis parcourt les cases non marquées (34–38). Le regroupement des écritures est un mécanisme d’optimisation possible; le code seul ne démontre pas qu’il améliore le temps.

hypotheses.claim: Un bitmap compact des impairs pourrait réduire le temps complet par rapport au vecteur d’octets actuel, mais le coût des opérations sur bits peut annuler ce bénéfice à la borne fixe.

observations.claim: L’essai f044 est rapporté valide et correct, avec un temps moyen de 0,0039508155 s et un score de 0,9076873. Le baseline visible est aussi rapporté valide et correct, à 0,0388473586 s; ces mesures ne suffisent pas à attribuer un effet causal à une partie du code.

uncertainties: La page de catalogue à l’offset 18 et les éventuels éléments qu’elle contient ne sont pas présents dans les pages fournies; je ne peux donc pas classer tous les essais.
Les échantillons bruts et une confirmation en cinq répétitions pour f044 ne sont pas visibles.

code_findings.mechanism: La variante f48 parcourt les résidus copremiers à 30, somme les candidats premiers et ne stocke comme diviseurs que ceux satisfaisant candidate <= limit/candidate. Ainsi, elle évite de conserver les premiers qui ne pourraient diviser aucun candidat jusqu’à limit. Son arrêt de boucle utilise divisor*divisor > candidate; dans le contrat borné à 200000, les diviseurs stockés sont au plus sqrt(limit), donc le produit reste représentable en int. Ce mécanisme est établi par le code; son effet sur le temps ou la mémoire n’est pas isolé.

Dans les deux versions, le parcours et le stockage sont identiques dans les extraits; la condition d’arrêt diffère: 68ad compare divisor à candidate/divisor, f48 compare divisor*divisor à candidate. Cela rend possible un test isolé du coût des deux formes, mais les moyennes observées seules ne prouvent pas que cette différence cause un gain.

403 utilise un vecteur de uint16_t et une roue parcourue par écarts; f48 utilise un vecteur de int et des blocs/résidus. Le type uint16_t peut réduire la taille des éléments stockés, mais ni la mémoire de crête ni l’effet de ce choix isolé ne sont mesurés.

hypotheses.claim: À parcours identique, la condition d’arrêt par multiplication pourrait être plus rapide que celle par division; l’écart mesuré ne suffit pas à l’établir.
hypotheses.proposed_test: Comparer deux variantes ne différant que par cette condition, passer tous les tests, le benchmark fixe avec le protocole habituel, puis les cinq répétitions de confirmation.
hypotheses.stop_condition: Rejeter la variante si un test échoue ou si les confirmations ne montrent pas une baisse reproductible du temps.

hypotheses.claim: Le stockage uint16_t pourrait être un compromis mémoire utile, même si la variante 403 a une moyenne légèrement plus élevée que f48.
hypotheses.proposed_test: Depuis f48, ne changer que le type des éléments stockés en uint16_t; mesurer la mémoire de crête et le temps, avec les tests et benchmark fixes puis cinq confirmations.
hypotheses.stop_condition: Rejeter si un test échoue ou si la mémoire de crête ne baisse pas; si elle baisse mais que le temps augmente, ne retenir que comme compromis mémoire/temps.
